danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 9
paragraphs: Fyrst Andrej nåede hærens hovedkvarter i slutningen af juni. Den første armé, som kejseren var hos, lå i den befæstede lejr ved Drissa; den anden armé var under tilbagetog og forsøgte at forene sig med den første, hvorfra den sagdes at være afskåret af store franske styrker. Alle var utilfredse med den generelle gang i den russiske hær, men ingen forudså nogen fare for en invasion af de russiske provinser, og ingen troede, at krigen ville strække sig længere end til de vestlige, de polske provinser.

Fyrst Andrej fandt Barclay de Tolly, som han var tildelt, ved bredden af Drissa. Da der ikke var en eneste by eller større landsby i lejrens nærhed, boede det vældige antal generaler og hoffolk, der fulgte hæren, i de bedste huse i landsbyerne på begge sider af floden i en radius af ti kilometer. Barclay de Tolly var indkvarteret næsten fem kilometer fra kejseren. Han modtog Bolkonskij stift og koldt og sagde med sin udenlandske accent, at han ville nævne ham for kejseren med henblik på en beslutning om hans ansættelse, men bad ham imidlertid forblive ved sin stab. Anatole Kurágin, som fyrst Andrej havde håbet at finde ved hæren, var ikke der. Han var rejst til Petersborg, men fyrst Andrej var glad for at høre det. Hans sind var optaget af den interesse, som den centrale ledelse af en gigantisk krig rummede, og han var glad for i en periode at være fri for den afledning, tanken om Kurágin forårsagede. I de første fire dage, mens ingen pligter krævedes af ham, red fyrst Andrej rundt i hele den befæstede lejr og forsøgte ved hjælp af sin egen viden og samtaler med eksperter at danne sig en bestemt mening om den. Men spørgsmålet om, hvorvidt lejren var fordelagtig eller ufordelagtig, forblev uafklaret for ham. Han var allerede ud fra sin militære erfaring og hvad han havde set under det østrigske felttog nået til den slutning, at de mest dybtgående planer i krig ingen betydning har, og at alt afhænger af, hvordan og af hvem fjendens uventede bevægelser — som ikke kan forudses — mødes. For at klare dette sidste punkt for sig selv forsøgte fyrst Andrej med sin stilling og sine bekendtskaber at gennemskue karakteren af hærens ledelse og de mænd og partier, der var involveret, og han udledte følgende billede af forholdene.

Mens kejseren endnu havde været i Vilna, var styrkerne blevet delt i tre arméer. For det første armeen under Barclay de Tolly, for det andet armeen under Bagratión, og for det tredje den under Tormásovs kommando. Kejseren var hos den første armé, men ikke som øverstkommanderende. I de udstedte ordrer stod der ikke, at kejseren ville overtage kommandoen, men kun at han ville være hos armeen. Kejseren havde desuden ikke en øverstkommanderende stab, men den kejserlige hovedkvarterstab. I hans følge var chefen for den kejserlige stab, generalkvartermester fyrst Volkónskij, samt generaler, kejserlige adjudanter, diplomatiske embedsmænd og et stort antal udlændinge, men ikke arméstaben. Foruden disse var der i kejserens følge uden nogen bestemt udnævnelse: Araktjejev, den tidligere krigsminister; grev Bennigsen, den rangmæssigt ældste general; storfyrst Tsarévitj Konstantin Pávlovitj; grev Rumjántsev, kansleren; Stein, en tidligere preussisk minister; Armfeldt, en svensk general; Pfuel, hovedmanden bag felttogsplanen; Paulucci, en generaladjudant og sardiniansk emigrant; Wolzogen — og mange andre. Selv om disse mænd ikke havde nogen militær udnævnelse i hæren, gav deres stilling dem indflydelse, og ofte vidste en korpskommandør eller endda den øverstkommanderende ikke, i hvilken egenskab han blev udspurgt af Bennigsen, storfyrsten, Araktjejev eller fyrst Volkónskij, eller modtog dette eller hint råd, og heller ikke om en bestemt ordre, der var modtaget i form af et råd, stammede fra den mand, der gav det, eller fra kejseren, og om den skulle udføres eller ej. Men dette var kun den ydre betingelse; den egentlige betydning af kejserens og alle disse menneskers tilstedeværelse var — set fra en hofmands synspunkt (og i en kejsers nærhed blev alle hofmænd) — klar for enhver. Den var denne: kejseren påtog sig ikke titlen øverstkommanderende, men rådede over alle hærene; mændene omkring ham var hans medhjælpere. Araktjejev var en trofast vogter, der sørgede for orden, og fungerede som regentens livvagt. Bennigsen var en godsejer i Vilna-provinsen, der syntes at gøre honnør for egnen, men i virkeligheden var en god general, nyttig som rådgiver og klar til at afløse Barclay. Storfyrsten var der, fordi det passede ham. Den forhenværende minister Stein var der, fordi hans råd var nyttigt, og fordi kejser Aleksandr holdt ham personligt i høj agtelse. Armfeldt nærede et voldsomt had til Napoleon og var en general fuld af selvtillid, en egenskab der altid påvirkede Aleksandr. Paulucci var der, fordi han var dristig og bestemt i sin tale. Generaladjudanterne var der, fordi de altid fulgte kejseren, og endelig og først og fremmest var Pfuel der, fordi han havde udarbejdet felttogsplanen mod Napoleon, og fordi han havde fået Aleksandr til at tro på dens virkning og ledte hele krigens gang. Hos Pfuel var Wolzogen, der udtrykte Pfuels tanker på en mere forståelig måde, end Pfuel selv — der var en barsk, boglig teoretiker, selvsikker i en grad, så han foragtede alle andre — formåede.

Foruden disse russere og udlændinge, der dagligt fremsatte nye og uventede idéer — især udlændingene, der gjorde det med den dristighed, som er karakteristisk for folk ansat i et land, der ikke er deres eget — var der mange sekundære personager, der fulgte hæren, fordi deres principaler var der.
Blandt de meninger og stemmer i denne vældige, rastløse, strålende og stolte sfære bemærkede fyrst Andrej følgende skarpt afgrænsede undergrupper af tendenser og partier:

Det første parti bestod af Pfuel og hans tilhængere — militærteoretikere, der troede på en krigsvidenskab med uforanderlige love — love om skrå bevægelser, omgåelser og lignende. Pfuel og hans tilhængere krævede en tilbagetrækning ind i landets indre i overensstemmelse med præcise love fastlagt af en pseudoteori om krig, og de så kun barbari, uvidenhed eller ond vilje i enhver afvigelse fra denne teori. Til dette parti hørte de udenlandske adelige, Wolzogen, Wintzingerode og andre, hovedsageligt tyskere.

Det andet parti var direkte modsat det første; den ene yderlighed blev som altid mødt af repræsentanter for den anden. Medlemmerne af dette parti var dem, der havde krævet en fremrykning fra Vilna ind i Polen og frihed fra alle forud fastlagte planer. Ud over at være fortalere for dristig handling repræsenterede denne gruppe også nationalisme, hvilket gjorde dem endnu mere ensidige i striden. De var russere: Bagratión, Jermólov (der var begyndt at gøre sig gældende) og andre. På det tidspunkt cirkulerede en berømt vittighed af Jermólov om, at han som en stor nådesbevisning havde anmodet kejseren om at gøre ham til tysker. Mændene i dette parti sagde, idet de mindedes Suvórov, at det, man skulle gøre, ikke var at ræsonnere eller stikke nåle i kort, men at kæmpe, slå fjenden, holde ham ude af Rusland og ikke lade hæren miste modet.

Til det tredje parti — hvortil kejseren havde størst tillid — hørte de hoffolk, der forsøgte at arrangere kompromiser mellem de to andre. Medlemmerne af dette parti, hovedsageligt civile og blandt hvem Araktjejev hørte, tænkte og sagde, hvad folk der ingen overbevisning har men gerne vil synes at have det, normalt siger. De sagde, at krig, særlig mod et geni som Bonaparte (de kaldte ham Bonaparte nu), ganske vist kræver de mest dybtgående planer og dyb videnskabelig indsigt, og i den henseende var Pfuel et geni, men man måtte samtidig erkende, at teoretikere ofte er ensidige, og at man derfor ikke blindt burde stole på dem, men også lytte til, hvad Pfuels modstandere og praktiske krigserfarede folk havde at sige, og så vælge en mellemvej. De insisterede på at bevare lejren ved Drissa i henhold til Pfuels plan, men ændre de øvrige hæres bevægelser. Selv om hverken det ene eller det andet mål herved kunne nås, syntes det dog bedst for tilhængerne af dette tredje parti.

Af et fjerde synspunkt var den mest fremtrædende repræsentant tsarévitjen, der ikke kunne glemme sin skuffelse ved Austerlitz, hvor han havde redet ud i spidsen for Garden i hjelm og kavaleriuniform som til en parade og forventet at knuse franskmændene glansfuldt; men uventet fandt sig i forreste linje og med nød og næppe undslap i den almindelige forvirring. Mændene i dette parti havde både den egenskab og den mangel at være åbenhjertige i deres meninger. De frygtede Napoleon, anerkendte hans styrke og deres egen svaghed og sagde det ligeud. De sagde: »Intet andet end sorg, skam og ruin vil komme ud af alt dette! Vi har opgivet Vilna og Vítebsk og vil opgive Drissa. Det eneste fornuftige, der er tilbage at gøre, er at slutte fred så hurtigt som muligt, inden vi bliver jaget ud af Petersborg.«
Denne opfattelse var meget udbredt i hærens øverste kredse og fandt også støtte i Petersborg og hos kansleren Rumjántsev, der af andre statslige grunde gik ind for fred.

Det femte parti bestod af tilhængere af Barclay de Tolly, ikke så meget som person, men som krigsminister og øverstkommanderende. »Vær han som han vil« (de begyndte altid sådan), »er han en ærlig, praktisk mand, og vi har ingen bedre. Giv ham virkelig magt, for krig kan ikke føres med held uden enhed i kommandoen, og han vil vise, hvad han kan, som han gjorde i Finland. Hvis vor hær er godt organiseret og stærk og har trukket sig tilbage til Drissa uden at lide nederlag, skylder vi udelukkende Barclay det. Hvis Barclay nu skal afløses af Bennigsen, går alt tabt, for Bennigsen viste sin uduelighed allerede i 1807.«

Det sjette parti, Bennigsens tilhængere, sagde derimod, at der i hvert fald ikke fandtes nogen mere aktiv og erfaren end Bennigsen: »og drej og vend jer som I vil, I ender hos Bennigsen. Lad de andre begå fejl nu!« sagde de og argumenterede for, at vor tilbagetrækning til Drissa var det skammeligste tilbagetog og en ubrudt række af fejl. »Jo flere fejl der begås, des bedre. Det vil i det mindste hurtigere blive forstået, at det ikke kan fortsætte sådan. Hvad der trengs, er ikke nogen Barclay eller hvem som helst, men en mand som Bennigsen, der gjorde sig gældende i 1807, og som Napoleon selv ydede retfærdighed — en mand, hvis autoritet frivilligt ville blive anerkendt, og Bennigsen er den eneste af den slags.«

Det syvende parti bestod af den slags mennesker, der altid findes, især omkring unge herskere, og som der var særlig mange af omkring Aleksandr — generaler og kejserlige adjudanter, lidenskabeligt hengivne til kejseren, ikke blot som monark, men som menneske, der oprigtigt og uselvisk tilbad ham, som Rostov havde gjort i 1805, og som i ham så ikke alene alle dyder, men også alle menneskelige evner. Disse mænd var, skønt henrykte over regentens afvisning af at kommandere hæren, alligevel utilfredse med hans overdrevne beskedenhed og ønskede og insisterede kun på, at deres tilbedte regent skulle opgive sin tilbageholdenhed og åbent erklære, at han ville stille sig i spidsen for hæren, samle en øverstkommanderende-stab omkring sig og, idet han rådførte sig med erfarne teoretikere og praktikere, hvor det var nødvendigt, selv føre tropperne, hvis ånd derved ville blive hævet til det højeste.

Det ottende og største parti, der i sine enorme tal var for de andre som nioghalvfems til én, bestod af mænd, der hverken ønskede fred eller krig, hverken fremrykning eller forsvarslejr ved Drissa eller noget andet sted, hverken Barclay eller kejseren, hverken Pfuel eller Bennigsen, men kun det ene mest væsentlige — så mange fordele og fornøjelser for sig selv som muligt. I de urolige vande af modstridende og krydsende intriger, der hvirvlede omkring kejserens hovedkvarter, var det muligt at have held med sig på måder, der var utænkelige til andre tider. En mand, der simpelthen ønskede at beholde sin lukrative post, ville i dag give Pfuel ret, i morgen hans modstander, og dagen derpå, blot for at undgå ansvar eller behage kejseren, erklære at han slet ingen mening havde i sagen. En anden, der ønskede at opnå en fordel, ville tiltrække kejserens opmærksomhed ved højlydt at forkæmpe netop det, kejseren havde antydet dagen før, og ville skændes og råbe i rådet, slå sig for brystet og udfordre dem, der ikke var enige med ham, til duel og derved bevise, at han var rede til at ofre sig for det almene vel. En tredje ville, i fraværet af modstandere, mellem to rådsmøder simpelthen anmode om en særlig gratifikation for sin trofaste tjeneste, vel vidende at folk i det øjeblik ville være for travlt optaget til at afslå ham. En fjerde, selv om han tilsyneladende var overbebyrdet med arbejde, ville jævnligt komme »tilfældigt« forbi kejserens blik. En femte ville, for at opnå sit længe nærede mål om at spise middag med kejseren, hårdnakket insistere på rigtigheden eller fejlagtigheden af et nyt synspunkt og til det formål fremføre argumenter af mere eller mindre overbevisende karakter.

Alle mænd i dette parti fiskede efter rubler, ordener og forfremmelser, og i denne jagt fulgte de kun den kejserlige nådes vejrhane, og så snart de bemærkede, at den drejede i en retning, begyndte hele denne hærs dronebefolkning at blæse kraftigt den vej, så det blev des sværere for kejseren at vende den andetsteds hen. Midt i usikkerheden om stillingen, med truslen om alvorlig fare der gav et særligt truende præg over alt, midt i denne malstrøm af intriger, egoisme, sammenstød af synspunkter og følelser og mangfoldighed af racer blandt disse mennesker — tilførte dette ottende og største parti af folk, der var optaget af personlige interesser, stor forvirring og uklarhed til den fælles sag. Uanset hvilket spørgsmål der opstod, fløj en sværm af disse droner, uden at have afsluttet deres summen om et tidligere emne, over til det nye og overdøvede og formørkede med deres summen stemmerne fra dem, der ærligt debatterede.

Af alle disse partier dannede der sig netop på det tidspunkt, fyrst Andrej nåede hæren, endnu et, et niende parti, der begyndte at hæve sin stemme. Dette var de ældres parti, fornuftige, erfarne og i statsanliggender kyndige mænd, der uden at dele nogen af disse modstridende meninger var i stand til at anlægge et udefrakommende blik på, hvad der foregik ved staben i hovedkvarteret, og overveje udveje af dette virvar, denne ubeslutsomhed, forvikling og svaghed.

Mændene i dette parti sagde og mente, at det, der gik galt, hovedsageligt skyldtes kejserens tilstedeværelse ved hæren med sit militære hof og den deraf følgende tilstedeværelse af en ubestemt, betinget og ustabil svingning af forbindelser, der passer ved et hof, men er skadelig i en hær; at en regent bør regere, men ikke kommandere hæren, og at den eneste udvej ville være, at kejseren og hans hof forlod hæren; at selve kejserens tilstedeværelse lammede handlekraften hos halvtreds tusind mand, der var nødvendige for at sikre hans personlige sikkerhed, og at den dårligste øverstkommanderende, hvis blot han var uafhængig, ville være bedre end den allerbedste, der var hæmmet af monarkens nærhed og autoritet.

Netop på det tidspunkt, da fyrst Andrej boede uden beskæftigelse i Drissa, skrev Sjisjkóv, statssekretæren og en af dette partis fornemste repræsentanter, et brev til kejseren, som Araktjejev og Balasjov indvilligede i at underskrive. I dette brev foreslog han, idet han benyttede sig af den tilladelse, kejseren havde givet ham til at drøfte den generelle krigsgang, ærbødigt — med den begrundelse at det var nødvendigt for regenten at vække krigsånd hos hovedstadens befolkning — at kejseren skulle forlade hæren.

Denne vækken af folket ved regentens hånd og hans kald til dem om at forsvare deres fædreland — den selvsamme tilskyndelse, der i den grad den blev fremkaldt af tsarens personlige tilstedeværelse i Moskva, var hovedårsagen til Ruslands triumf — blev foreslået kejseren og accepteret af ham som et påskud for at forlade hæren.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Prince Andrew reached army headquarters at the end of June. The first army, with which was the Emperor, occupied the fortified camp at Drissa; the second army was retreating, trying to join up with the first, from which it was said to be cut off by large French forces. Everyone was dissatisfied with the general course of affairs in the Russian army, but no one anticipated any danger of invasion of the Russian provinces, and no one thought the war would extend farther than the western, Polish, provinces.

Prince Andrew found Barclay de Tolly, to whom he had been assigned, on the bank of the Drissa. As there was not a single town or large village in the vicinity of the camp, the immense number of generals and courtiers accompanying the army were living in the best houses of villages on both sides of the river, over a radius of six miles. Barclay de Tolly was quartered nearly three miles from the Emperor. He received Bolkonsky stiffly and coldly and told him in his foreign accent that he would mention him to the Emperor for a decision on his assignment, but asked him meanwhile to remain on his staff. Anatole Kuragin, whom Prince Andrew had hoped to find with the army, was not there. He had gone to Petersburg, but Prince Andrew was glad to hear this. His mind was occupied with the affairs of the great center that was conducting a gigantic war, and he was glad to be free for a while from the distraction caused by thoughts of Kuragin. During the first four days, while no duties were required of him, Prince Andrew rode all around the fortified camp and, using his own knowledge and his conversations with experts, tried to form a definite opinion about it. But the question of whether the camp was advantageous or not remained unresolved in his mind. Already from his military experience and from what he had seen in the Austrian campaign, he had reached the conclusion that in war the most carefully considered plans have no significance and that everything depends on how unexpected movements of the enemy — which cannot be foreseen — are met, and on how and by whom the whole matter is handled. To understand this last point, Prince Andrew, using his position and connections, tried to grasp the character of the army's leadership and of the men and factions involved, and he arrived at the following picture of the situation.

While the Emperor had still been at Vilna, the forces had been divided into three armies. First, the army under Barclay de Tolly; second, the army under Bagration; and third, the one commanded by Tormasov. The Emperor was with the first army, but not as commander in chief. In the orders issued, it was not stated that the Emperor would take command, only that he would be with the army. The Emperor moreover had with him not a commander in chief's staff but the imperial headquarters staff. In attendance on him was the head of the imperial staff, Quartermaster General Prince Volkonsky, as well as generals, imperial aides-de-camp, diplomatic officials, and a large number of foreigners — but not the army staff. Besides these, there were in attendance on the Emperor without any definite assignments: Arakcheev, the former Minister of War; Count Bennigsen, the senior general by rank; the Grand Duke Tsarevich Constantine Pavlovich; Count Rumyantsev, the Chancellor; Stein, a former Prussian minister; Armfeldt, a Swedish general; Pfuel, the chief author of the plan of campaign; Paulucci, an adjutant general and Sardinian emigre; Wolzogen — and many others. Though these men held no military position in the army, their standing gave them influence, and often a corps commander, or even the commander in chief, didn't know whether a certain question from Bennigsen, the Grand Duke, Arakcheev, or Prince Volkonsky was the questioner's own idea or the Emperor's, and whether or not a given order received in the form of advice had to be obeyed. But this was only the surface; the essential significance of the Emperor's presence and of all these people, from a courtier's perspective (and in an Emperor's vicinity all became courtiers), was clear to everyone. It was this: the Emperor did not take the title of commander in chief but controlled all the armies; the men around him were his assistants. Arakcheev was a faithful enforcer of order who served as the sovereign's bodyguard. Bennigsen was a landowner in the Vilna province who appeared to be doing the honors of the district but was actually a competent general, useful as an adviser and ready to replace Barclay. The Grand Duke was there because it suited him. The former Minister Stein was there because his advice was valuable and Emperor Alexander held him in high personal esteem. Armfeldt bitterly hated Napoleon and was a general full of self-confidence — a quality that always influenced Alexander. Paulucci was there because he was bold and decisive in speech. The adjutants general were there because they always accompanied the Emperor, and lastly and chiefly, Pfuel was there because he had drawn up the plan of campaign against Napoleon and, having persuaded Alexander to believe in its effectiveness, was directing the whole business of the war. With Pfuel was Wolzogen, who expressed Pfuel's thoughts in a more comprehensible way than Pfuel himself — who was a harsh, bookish theorist, self-confident to the point of despising everyone else — could manage.

Besides these Russians and foreigners who proposed new and unexpected ideas every day — especially the foreigners, who did so with the boldness characteristic of people working in a country not their own — there were many lesser figures accompanying the army because their principals were there.
Among the opinions and voices in this immense, restless, brilliant, and proud sphere, Prince Andrew noticed the following clearly defined factions and tendencies:

The first faction consisted of Pfuel and his followers — military theorists who believed in a science of war with immutable laws governing oblique movements, flanking maneuvers, and so forth. Pfuel and his followers demanded a retreat into the depths of the country in accordance with the precise laws of their pseudo-science of war, and they saw only barbarism, ignorance, or evil intent in every deviation from that theory. To this faction belonged the foreign nobles — Wolzogen, Wintzingerode, and others, chiefly Germans.

The second faction was the direct opposite of the first; as always, one extreme was met by representatives of the other. Its members demanded an advance from Vilna into Poland and freedom from all prearranged plans. Besides advocating bold action, this group also represented nationalism, which made them still more one-sided in the dispute. They were Russians: Bagration, Ermolov (who was beginning to come to prominence), and others. At that time a famous joke of Ermolov's was circulating: as a great favor he had supposedly petitioned the Emperor to make him a German. The men of this faction, invoking the memory of Suvorov, said that what one had to do was not theorize or stick pins in maps, but fight, beat the enemy, keep him out of Russia, and not let the army get demoralized.

The third faction — in which the Emperor had the most confidence — consisted of courtiers who tried to arrange compromises between the other two. Its members, chiefly civilians (including Arakcheev), thought and said what men who have no convictions but wish to appear to have some generally say. They said that undoubtedly war, particularly against such a genius as Bonaparte (they now called him Bonaparte), requires the most deeply considered plans and profound scientific knowledge, and in that respect Pfuel was a genius, but at the same time one had to acknowledge that theorists are often one-sided, and therefore one shouldn't rely on them absolutely but should also listen to what Pfuel's opponents and practical men experienced in warfare had to say, and then choose a middle course. They insisted on keeping the camp at Drissa, according to Pfuel's plan, but on altering the movements of the other armies. Though by this approach neither one aim nor the other could be attained, it seemed best to the members of this third faction.

The most conspicuous representative of the fourth faction was the Tsarevich, who could not forget his disillusionment at Austerlitz, where he had ridden out at the head of the Guards in his helmet and cavalry uniform as to a review, expecting to crush the French gallantly, but had unexpectedly found himself in the front line and had narrowly escaped amid the general confusion. The men of this faction had both the virtue and the defect of frankness. They feared Napoleon, recognized his strength and their own weakness, and openly said so. They said: "Nothing but sorrow, shame, and ruin will come of all this! We have abandoned Vilna and Vitebsk and shall abandon Drissa. The only sensible thing left is to make peace as soon as possible, before we are thrown out of Petersburg."
This view was widely held in the upper army circles and found support also in Petersburg and from the Chancellor, Rumyantsev, who for other reasons of state favored peace.

The fifth faction consisted of supporters of Barclay de Tolly, not so much of the man as of the minister of war and commander in chief. "Be he what he may" (they always began like that), "he is an honest, practical man and we have nobody better. Give him real power, for war cannot be waged successfully without unity of command, and he will show what he can do, as he did in Finland. If our army is well organized and strong and has retreated to Drissa without suffering any defeats, we owe this entirely to Barclay. If Barclay is now replaced by Bennigsen, all will be lost, for Bennigsen proved his incompetence as far back as 1807."

The sixth faction, the Bennigsenites, said on the contrary that there was certainly no one more active and experienced than Bennigsen: "Twist about as you may, you'll have to come to Bennigsen in the end. Let the others make mistakes now!" said they, arguing that our retreat to Drissa was a most shameful reverse and an unbroken chain of blunders. "The more mistakes that are made the better. At least it will be understood sooner that things can't go on like this. What is needed is not some Barclay or other, but a man like Bennigsen, who proved himself in 1807 and to whom Napoleon himself gave credit — a man whose authority would be willingly accepted, and Bennigsen is the only such man."

The seventh faction consisted of the sort of people who are always found around young sovereigns, and of whom there were particularly many around Alexander — generals and imperial aides-de-camp passionately devoted to the Emperor not merely as a monarch but as a man, adoring him sincerely and selflessly as Rostov had done in 1805, and who saw in him not only all the virtues but all human capabilities as well. These men, though delighted with the sovereign's refusal to command the army, nevertheless blamed him for such excessive modesty and only desired that their adored sovereign should abandon his diffidence and openly announce that he would take personal command of the army, gather a commander in chief's staff around him, and — consulting experienced theoreticians and practical men as needed — lead the troops himself, whose spirits would thereby be raised to the highest pitch.

The eighth and largest group, which outnumbered the others as ninety-nine to one, consisted of men who desired neither peace nor war, neither an advance nor a defensive camp at Drissa or anywhere else, neither Barclay nor the Emperor, neither Pfuel nor Bennigsen, but only the one most essential thing — as much advantage and pleasure for themselves as possible. In the troubled waters of conflicting and intersecting intrigues that swirled around the Emperor's headquarters, it was possible to succeed in many ways unthinkable at other times. A man who simply wanted to keep his lucrative post would today agree with Pfuel, tomorrow with his opponent, and the day after — merely to avoid responsibility or to please the Emperor — would declare that he had no opinion at all on the matter. Another who wished to gain some advantage would attract the Emperor's attention by loudly advocating the very thing the Emperor had hinted at the day before, and would argue and shout at the council, beating his chest and challenging those who disagreed to duels, thereby proving his readiness to sacrifice himself for the common good. A third, between two councils, would simply ask for a special bonus for his faithful services, well knowing that at such a moment people would be too busy to refuse. A fourth would keep arranging to appear accidentally before the Emperor's eyes. A fifth, to achieve his long-cherished aim of dining with the Emperor, would stubbornly argue for or against some newly emerging opinion and produce more or less convincing arguments to that end.

All the men of this group were fishing for decorations, promotions, and money, and in this pursuit they watched only the weathercock of imperial favor; as soon as they noticed it turning in any direction, this whole drone population of the army began blowing hard that way, making it all the harder for the Emperor to turn it elsewhere. Amid the uncertainties of the situation, with the threat of serious danger lending a peculiarly menacing character to everything, amid this vortex of intrigue, self-interest, conflicting views and feelings, and the diversity of nationalities among these people, this eighth and largest group — the people preoccupied with personal gain — introduced great confusion and obscurity into the common task. Whatever question arose, a swarm of these drones, without having finished buzzing about the previous topic, flew to the new one and by their noise drowned out and obscured the voices of those who were arguing honestly.

From among all these factions, just at the time Prince Andrew reached the army, another — a ninth — was being formed and beginning to raise its voice. This was the party of older, reasonable men experienced and capable in state affairs, who were able to take a detached view of what was happening at headquarters and to consider ways out of this muddle, indecision, confusion, and weakness.

The men of this faction said and thought that the problems stemmed mainly from the Emperor's presence in the army with his military court and the resulting indefinite, conditional, and unstable web of relationships, which was appropriate at court but harmful in an army; that a sovereign should reign but not command the army, and that the only solution was for the Emperor and his court to leave; that the mere presence of the Emperor paralyzed fifty thousand men needed to guarantee his personal safety; and that the worst commander in chief acting independently would be better than the best one hampered by the presence and authority of the monarch.

Just at the time Prince Andrew was living idly at Drissa, Shishkov, the Secretary of State and one of the chief representatives of this faction, wrote a letter to the Emperor which Arakcheev and Balashev agreed to sign. In this letter, taking advantage of the permission given him by the Emperor to discuss the general course of affairs, he respectfully suggested — on the grounds that it was necessary for the sovereign to rouse the people of the capital to a warlike spirit — that the Emperor should leave the army.

This stirring of the people by their sovereign and his call to them to defend their country — the very move that was the chief cause of Russia's triumph, insofar as it was produced by the Tsar's personal presence in Moscow — was suggested to the Emperor and accepted by him as a pretext for leaving the army.
